passage: The case for an independent central bank is usually made in terms of temptation. Elected governments face voters at regular intervals, and before an election they are tempted to loosen money, buying a brief rise in output and employment at the price of higher inflation later. Because the public comes to anticipate this, it builds the expected inflation into wages and prices in advance, so that the boost to output never materialises and only the inflation remains. Handing monetary policy to an appointed body with a mandate for stable prices removes the temptation and makes promises of low inflation believable. The gain, on this account, lies in credibility rather than in any superior cleverness on the part of the officials.

Against this stands a democratic objection that is easy to underrate. Decisions about interest rates have large effects on the distribution of income and wealth, between borrowers and savers, between the owners of assets and those who live on wages, and between one region and another. In a democracy, choices with consequences of that kind are supposed to be made by people who can be removed at the ballot box. To delegate them, the objection runs, is to take out of public contest exactly the decisions that most need it.

Both positions are partly right, and the distance between them narrows once we ask what, precisely, has been delegated. Independence in the choice of instruments is not the same as independence in the choice of goals. A legislature can fix the target, an inflation rate for instance, and require the central bank to explain in public whenever it misses; that body then decides how to reach the target, and it alone sets the interest rate. This arrangement preserves the commitment that defeats electoral temptation while leaving the ends of policy with elected representatives, and it answers much of the democratic objection without surrendering the gain in credibility.

The settlement is stable, however, only while the mandate remains narrow. When central banks are asked in addition to secure financial stability, support employment, steer credit towards favoured sectors or manage the risks of a changing climate, the claim that they merely apply technical means to democratically chosen ends begins to wear thin, because deciding how to trade these goals off against one another is itself a political judgement. The more a central bank is asked to do, the weaker its claim to be left alone while doing it.

passage: For much of the modern period the doctrine of sovereignty was understood as a wall. Within its borders a state was answerable to no outside authority, and what it did to its own population, however terrible, was a matter of domestic jurisdiction. The rule had a defensible rationale. A world in which any power could enter another's territory whenever it disapproved of how that territory was governed would be a world of permanent intervention, in which the strong would always find reasons to correct the weak. Non-interference was less a tribute to the virtue of governments than a device for keeping their quarrels within bounds.

The atrocities of the late twentieth century made the wall look like a shield for murderers, and a new formula emerged to reconcile the old principle with the demand to act. Sovereignty, it was argued, is not a privilege but a responsibility: a state holds it on condition that it protects its people, and a state that massacres them, or cannot stop others from doing so, forfeits its claim to be left alone. The formula is elegant, because it seems to dissolve the conflict rather than adjudicate it. Intervention to stop mass killing no longer violates sovereignty, since the sovereignty in question has already been forfeited.

The elegance is partly an illusion. The formula does not remove the hard question but relocates it. Someone must still decide when a government has failed badly enough to forfeit its rights, and in practice that someone is usually the state or coalition proposing to intervene, which is to say a party with interests of its own in the outcome. The old doctrine at least gave a clear answer to the question of who may enter: nobody. The new one replaces that answer with a judgement, and judgements made by the powerful about the weak have a history that should make anyone cautious. It is not a cynical point that intervention has tended to occur where the interveners had strategic reasons to be and not elsewhere; it is an observation about how a discretionary rule will be used.

None of this is an argument for returning to the wall. A principle that obliged the world to watch a massacre it could stop would purchase order at a price few would accept once they had seen what it meant. The question is not whether sovereignty may ever yield, but how the decision that it should yield is to be made credible. Here the procedure matters as much as the facts. An intervention authorised by a broad body of states, through rules that apply to friends as well as to enemies, carries a legitimacy that one undertaken by a single power on its own assessment cannot, even when the atrocities alleged are equally real.

The difficulty is that procedure can fail in the other direction. The bodies most able to confer legitimacy are also those in which a single interested member can block action, and the insistence on proper authorisation can become a reason for doing nothing while the killing continues. There is no formula that escapes this. A world that refuses all unauthorised intervention will sometimes stand by when it should act, and a world that permits it will sometimes see intervention used as a pretext. The honest position is to admit that we are choosing which of these failures to risk, and to stop pretending that a change of vocabulary has spared us the choice.

passage: When a country lowers its barriers to imports, the gains and the losses arrive in very different forms. The gains are spread thinly across millions of households, each of which pays a little less for clothing, appliances or food, usually without noticing why. The losses fall heavily on a few: the workers of a particular mill, the shops that depended on their wages, the town whose tax base was the mill. A small saving that nobody notices is politically weightless; a closed factory is a photograph on the front page. Those who lose know exactly what they have lost and whom to blame, while those who gain rarely connect their small savings to a decision taken in a distant ministry. It is not surprising that the politics of trade so often seems out of proportion to its economics.

Economists have a standard reply. Because the total gains exceed the total losses, the winners could in principle compensate the losers and still come out ahead, so that everyone ends up better off. The argument is correct as arithmetic, and it is the foundation of the case that open trade raises national welfare. But the word that carries the weight is 'could'. A compensation that is possible but never paid is no comfort to the people who bore the losses, and to present it as though it settled the matter is to confuse a hypothetical with a policy.

Where governments have tried to pay, the record is unimpressive, though the reasons are instructive. Programmes reserved for workers who could prove that their jobs were lost to imports required them to establish a cause that is often impossible to isolate, since a plant may close because of foreign competition, new machinery and poor management all at once. Many eligible workers never applied; many who applied were retrained for occupations that were themselves shrinking. The failure lay less in the idea of compensation than in tying it to a cause that could not be reliably identified.

This suggests that the better course is not a trade-specific remedy at all but support that follows the worker regardless of why the job disappeared: insurance against lost earnings, help with moving to where work exists, and training linked to employers who are actually hiring. Such measures cannot be justified as payment for trade alone, and they will cost more than narrow programmes did. Yet the case for open trade has always rested on the claim that its benefits are broadly shared. If that claim is to be more than an assertion, the sharing has to be done by someone, and it will not happen by itself.

passage: Literary history has always been written from a remarkably small sample. Of the many thousands of novels published in a given century, a scholar can read a few hundred in a working life, and the histories of the form are built on a smaller set still, the books that later readers chose to keep in print. When such a history says that 'the novel' turned inward at a certain period, or abandoned the omniscient narrator, or grew preoccupied with the city, it is generalising from a selection that was never meant to be representative. Nobody chose the canon as a sample; it was assembled by generations of readers for reasons of taste, teaching and accident, and there is no reason to expect it to resemble the whole from which it was drawn. The advocates of computational or 'distant' reading start from this embarrassment. If machines can process an entire century's output, counting words, tracking the length of sentences or the frequency with which characters are named, then claims about the form as a whole can at last be tested against the whole.

The objections are familiar, and some are serious. Counting is not reading. The meaning of a word depends on its context, on irony, on the dramatic situation in which it is spoken, none of which a frequency table records. Critics add that many of the patterns such studies report are either trivial or confirm what attentive readers already knew, so that a great deal of machinery produces a modest result dressed in charts. There is also a subtler worry: the features a computer can count are those that can be defined mechanically, and these are not obviously the features that matter. A discipline that adopts such tools risks drifting towards studying what can be measured simply because it can be measured. Defenders of the method reply that every discipline begins by measuring crude things, but the reply concedes more than it denies.

Yet much of this debate rests on a false picture of the choice. Distant reading does not replace close reading so much as change what close reading is asked to do. Its most interesting results are rarely the patterns themselves; they are the anomalies, the decade in which a measure behaves unexpectedly or the obscure novels that cluster with canonical ones on some feature nobody had thought to examine. A measure that shows some habit of style rising steadily for decades and then collapsing within a few years explains nothing by itself, but it tells a scholar exactly where to look. Such a finding means little until someone goes back and reads the books in question, and it is that return which produces understanding. The count poses a question; it does not answer one.

Where the method does make an independent contribution is in the matter of the sample. Even if a computer can say little about what any single novel means, it can show that a generalisation drawn from the canon fails to hold for the much larger body of books that the canon left out. That is not a trivial service. A claim about what 'the novel' did, which turns out to describe only the few hundred books that survived into the syllabus, was never a claim about the novel at all, but about the tastes of the readers who did the selecting. The modest promise of distant reading, then, is less to tell us what literature means than to tell us more accurately which literature our claims are about.

passage: Two accounts of the professions have long competed for our assent, and each is right about something. The first, which professionals themselves favour, holds that a profession is defined by esoteric knowledge put at the service of clients who cannot judge it. Because a patient cannot assess a diagnosis or a litigant a legal argument, the state licenses practitioners, and the licence is a guarantee of competence that protects the public from charlatans. The second account, favoured by economists of a sceptical turn, treats the same licence as a barrier to entry: by limiting the number who may practise, a profession raises its fees, and its talk of public protection is simply the language in which a cartel describes itself.

What the two accounts share is more interesting than what divides them. Both look at one profession at a time, as if each stood alone facing its clients, and both assume that the work a profession does is simply given: there are diseases, so there are doctors; there are disputes, so there are lawyers. Yet the boundaries of professional work are anything but given. Whether persistent unhappiness is a medical condition, a psychological difficulty, a spiritual crisis or a social problem is not settled by the nature of unhappiness. It is settled, provisionally and repeatedly, by contests among psychiatrists, psychologists, clergy and social workers, each of whom claims that the problem properly belongs to it.

Seen from this angle, a profession is less a guild guarding a fixed territory than one party in a system of rival claims, and its history is a history of conquests and retreats. Licensing remains important, but as a weapon in a jurisdictional struggle rather than as either a certificate or a mere device for fixing prices. Knowledge, too, matters in a different way. What wins a contested problem is often not superior skill in treating it but a more abstract body of theory, one that allows a profession to redefine the problem in its own terms and so to argue that its rivals were treating the symptoms rather than the thing itself. A profession whose knowledge is purely practical can be displaced by one that can explain why that practice works.

This does not mean that competence is irrelevant or that the cartel theorist is merely cynical. Clients are protected by licensing, and fees are raised by it. But neither effect explains why some professions grow while others shrink, or why a body of practitioners who are perfectly good at their work can find that work quietly reassigned to others. The fate of a profession, on this view, depends less on how well it does what it does than on its ability to persuade others, including the state and the public, that the problems of the moment are its problems.

passage: The phrase 'guilty pleasure' has become one of the most common ways of talking about taste. A person confesses to loving a televised singing contest, a formulaic romance series or a song that dominated the charts in her teens, and the confession is offered with a smile that asks to be forgiven. On the surface the phrase is modest, even self-deprecating; looked at more closely, it does a surprising amount of work, and not all of that work is modest.

Consider what the speaker gains. By calling the pleasure guilty, she is able to enjoy the thing while signalling that she knows it is beneath her; she occupies the position of the enthusiast and the position of the critic at once. The confession is a kind of insurance: if her listener turns out to share the enthusiasm, nothing is lost; if the listener sneers, she has already sneered first. What looks like an admission of bad taste is therefore, very often, a display of good taste, since only someone who knows the rankings can confess to violating them.

This is why the phrase, for all its apparent humility, tends to preserve the hierarchy it seems to question. Every guilty pleasure implies an innocent one, a set of books, films and songs that may be enjoyed without apology because they are approved. The confession leaves that ranking intact; indeed it needs the ranking in order to mean anything. And the ranking itself is rarely examined. It is striking how often the pleasures labelled guilty are those associated with audiences who have little cultural prestige, the teenage, the provincial, the domestic, while the pleasures of the already respected are seldom described in this way, however predictable they may be.

It does not follow that no pleasure should ever make us uneasy. Some enjoyments really do deserve scrutiny: laughter at another person's humiliation, for instance, or the thrill of watching real suffering staged for entertainment. But in those cases the unease concerns what the pleasure does or endorses, not where its object sits in a ranking of prestige, and the honest response is to ask what we are enjoying and why. That question is worth asking of the singing contest as well. Perhaps the answer will be that it offers something real, the spectacle of ordinary people attempting something difficult in public. If so, the pleasure needs no apology; if not, a shrug and a smile will not settle the matter either.

passage: The word improvisation tends to conjure an image of pure spontaneity: a musician who sits down with nothing prepared and lets whatever arrives come out. Listeners who admire improvisers often praise them in exactly these terms, as if the value of the performance lay in its having come from nowhere. Yet the image badly misdescribes what improvising musicians actually do. In the classical traditions of the Indian subcontinent, a performer exploring a raga is bound by an intricate set of expectations: which notes may be used, how the scale is approached in ascent and in descent, which phrases characterise the raga and which would make it sound like a neighbouring one. A jazz soloist working through a familiar tune is likewise held by the sequence of chords beneath the melody, by the length of each chorus and by a large shared stock of phrases that players absorb over years of listening.

What these traditions share is not an absence of rules but a particular relation to them. The improviser has internalised the constraints so thoroughly that they no longer need to be consulted; they shape choices in the way grammar shapes the sentences of a fluent speaker, who does not pause to recall the rules before talking. The comparison with language is useful because it removes an apparent paradox. Nobody thinks that a conversation is unoriginal because it obeys grammar, and nobody thinks that grammar prevents people from saying things that have never been said before. On the contrary, it is the shared structure that makes a new sentence intelligible as new.

This has a practical consequence for how improvisation is learned. A student who is told simply to be free usually produces something shapeless, or falls back on a handful of habits picked up by accident. Teachers in both traditions instead begin with imitation: the student copies phrases, sometimes for years, until the vocabulary becomes second nature. To an outsider this can look like the opposite of creativity. But imitation here is the means by which the constraints are absorbed, and only once they have been absorbed can the student vary them with confidence.

None of this is to say that improvisation is merely the recombination of stored parts, or that the best improvisers are simply those with the largest memories. What listeners value in a great performance is often a moment at which a convention is stretched or bent in a way that still makes sense within the tradition, so that the surprise is felt as a surprise. Such moments are possible only for someone who knows exactly where the boundaries lie. Freedom in improvisation, in other words, is not freedom from form but a fluency so complete that form can be played with.

passage: Suppose a lender uses a scoring system to estimate how likely each applicant is to default, and suppose applicants belong to two groups that differ, for whatever historical reasons, in how often their members in fact default. There are several natural ways to ask whether the system treats the groups fairly. One may ask whether a given score means the same thing in both groups, so that among applicants scored as having a one-in-five chance of default, roughly one in five defaults whichever group they belong to. One may ask instead whether applicants who would in fact have repaid are wrongly refused at the same rate in both groups, or whether those who would in fact have defaulted are wrongly approved at the same rate. Each of these looks like a reasonable requirement, and each has been proposed as the meaning of fairness.

It turns out that they cannot, in general, all be satisfied together. When the groups' underlying default rates differ and the prediction is less than perfect, a score that means the same thing in both groups will produce different rates of error between them, in wrongful refusals, wrongful approvals or both, and equalising both kinds of error will make the same score mean different things in different groups. This is not a defect of any particular system that better engineering might remove; it follows from the arithmetic of prediction under unequal base rates. The finding was greeted in some quarters as a kind of scandal, and two conclusions were quickly drawn from it: that the idea of a fair algorithm is incoherent, or, conversely, that since some criterion must be chosen, the choice is a technical matter best left to the people who build the systems.

Both conclusions seem to me mistaken, and for related reasons. The impossibility does not show that fairness is incoherent; it shows that our everyday notion of fairness bundles together several demands that usually travel together and part company only under specific conditions. Discovering that two values can conflict is not the same as discovering that one of them is empty, any more than the occasional conflict between honesty and kindness shows that one of these is an illusion. Nor does the need to choose make the choice technical. Which criterion should give way depends on what the decision does to the people it touches: who bears the cost of being wrongly refused, how severe that cost is, and whether the different base rates are themselves the residue of earlier unfairness that the decision would perpetuate. Those are questions about harm and responsibility, not about arithmetic.

It is worth adding that the dilemma is not peculiar to algorithms. A loan officer who judges applicants by experience faces exactly the same trade-off whenever the groups differ in base rates; the officer simply does not have to declare which criterion is being sacrificed, and may not know. In this respect the formal analysis has done something valuable. By making the conflict explicit, it has turned a choice that was always being made silently into one that must be made in the open, and has removed the comfortable belief that a sufficiently careful decision maker could satisfy every reasonable demand at once. The danger is that the explicitness is squandered, that the choice is buried again inside the system, this time under a layer of technical vocabulary instead of a layer of personal discretion.

passage: Among the arguments made for nuclear deterrence, the strongest is also the simplest: when two states can each destroy the other, neither can hope to gain from a general war, and so neither starts one. Whatever its moral costs, a balance of terror of this kind has a claim to have kept the largest powers from fighting each other directly for a long time. But the logic that makes the largest war unthinkable may make smaller ones more thinkable, and this possibility, sometimes called the stability-instability paradox, deserves more attention than the reassuring half of the argument usually receives.

The reasoning runs as follows. If both sides are confident that neither will ever risk a nuclear exchange, then each can assume that a limited clash, whether a border skirmish, a proxy war or a raid by irregular forces, will stay limited. The fear that once restrained such ventures, the fear that they might spiral into catastrophe, is weakened precisely by the confidence that catastrophe will be avoided. Stability at the top of the ladder of escalation thus loosens the rungs near the bottom. A state that would never dare a full invasion may feel free to probe, provoke and nibble, reasoning that its opponent will not answer with anything that could lead to the unthinkable.

It is important to be precise about what this claims. It does not say that nuclear weapons cause small wars, which have many causes and were common long before such weapons existed. It says only that mutual deterrence can lower the perceived risk of low-level aggression and so remove one brake on it. Nor does the paradox operate automatically. Its force depends on how confident each side is that escalation can be controlled. Where leaders doubt that a skirmish can be kept small, the old fear returns, and with it some of the old caution.

The implication is uncomfortable for those who credit deterrence with keeping the peace. What deterrence may secure is not peace in general but the absence of one particular kind of war, while the violence that remains is pushed downward and outward, into contested borderlands and into the hands of proxies. That is no small achievement, given what the alternative might be, and nothing in the paradox implies that the world would be safer if the largest powers could once again contemplate fighting each other directly. But the achievement should be described accurately. A system that prevents catastrophe partly by making lesser conflicts safer to start is not a system of peace; it is a way of choosing which wars will be fought.

passage: Few environmental gestures are as photogenic as planting a tree. A minister kneels with a spade, a schoolchild pats soil around a sapling, and a campaign announces that so many million trees have gone into the ground this season. The appeal is easy to understand. A tree is a visible, countable object, and counting is what campaigns need: a target can be set, met and reported. Yet the habit of measuring forest recovery by the number of saplings planted has quietly confused an input with an outcome, and the confusion has consequences for the land it is meant to help.

The first problem is survival. A sapling planted in the wrong season, in compacted soil or without anyone to water it through its first dry months often dies within a year or two, and a campaign that counts plantings rather than living trees will never record the loss. The second problem is choice. Large drives tend to favour a few fast-growing species that nurseries can raise cheaply and in bulk, and the result, where the saplings do survive, may be closer to a plantation than a forest: rows of a single kind of tree, offering little to the insects, birds and fungi that a mixed woodland supports. In some places such planting has even been carried out on grasslands that were never forested at all, replacing one valuable habitat with a poor imitation of another.

An alternative, less dramatic and much harder to photograph, is to let forests come back on their own. On land where old roots, nearby seed-bearing trees and a living soil remain, simply protecting an area from grazing, fire and clearing can allow a varied forest to regenerate, often more cheaply than planting and with species suited to the site because they arrived there by themselves. Regeneration of this kind is slow at first, and for some years the land looks like scrub, which is one reason it is undervalued: it does not look like progress.

None of this means that planting is always a mistake. Where soils are badly degraded, where no seed sources survive nearby, or where a particular species must be reintroduced, careful planting may be the only way to begin. The objection is not to the spade but to the scoreboard. A campaign that measured success by the area of land that becomes, and remains, a functioning forest after ten or twenty years would sometimes plant and sometimes refrain, and it would be judged by what grew rather than by what was put into the ground.

passage: It is easy to write the history of urban smell as a simple story of progress. Pre-modern cities stank of sewage, tanneries, slaughterhouses and unwashed bodies; reformers built drains and water supplies; the stench retreated. Every part of this is true, and anyone inclined to romanticise the crowded streets of earlier centuries should be reminded of it. But the story assumes that the nose is a constant instrument, registering the same smells with the same disgust in every age, and that assumption does not survive a reading of the sources.

Residents of older towns certainly complained about smells, but their complaints were selective. Odours that later generations would find unbearable, such as the smell of a dung heap beside a house, were often accepted as part of ordinary life, while others, associated with particular trades or with neighbours who were disliked, drew sustained protest. What made a smell intolerable depended less on its strength than on what it was thought to mean. And from the late eighteenth century onwards, in much of Europe, smells came to mean something very specific. Under the theory that disease spread through foul air, a bad smell was not merely unpleasant; it was a warning, perhaps even the danger itself.

The theory was wrong, but it was productive. Because it identified smell with sickness, it gave reformers a reason, and a sense of urgency, to remove the sources of smell, and many of the measures they took, from covered sewers to the regular removal of refuse, did reduce disease, though for reasons they did not understand. A mistaken idea about how illness spread thus helped to justify works whose real benefit lay elsewhere. When the germ theory displaced it, smell lost its medical authority; it did not lose its power.

Freed from medicine, the vocabulary of smell attached itself more firmly to persons. Middle-class households that had learned to fear foul air now learned to fear the odour of the poor, the newcomer and the manual worker, and the judgement passed easily from bodies to character. The cleaner cities became, the more a lingering smell could serve as a mark of social distance. This is why a history of smell cannot be only a history of drains; it must also be a history of who was allowed to call whom offensive, and of how a sense that seems the most immediate of all has always been schooled.

passage: It is often said that the phonograph and its successors simply made music available, carrying performances that had been confined to concert halls into the homes of people who would never have heard them. The claim is true as far as it goes, and the gain it describes is enormous: a listener in a small town can now hear more music in a month than a devoted concertgoer of earlier centuries could hope to hear in years. But the image of recording as a window, through which the listener observes a performance that would have happened in much the same way anyway, conceals the way recording altered both the performance and the act of listening.

Consider first what repetition does. A live performance is heard once; its slips pass and are forgotten, and its moments of risk are experienced as risk. A recording is heard again and again, and on the tenth hearing a wrong note or a wavering tone is no longer a passing accident but a permanent blemish. Performers who recorded learned that what was acceptable, even exciting, in a hall could become intolerable on disc. As editing techniques improved, it became possible to assemble a single flawless performance from many takes, and the flawless performance became the standard against which the live one was measured.

Listeners, in turn, came to the concert hall carrying recordings in their heads. Many now know a work first, and sometimes only, through one recorded interpretation, and they hear a live performance as a departure from it. This is a curious inversion. The recording was meant to be a copy of the performance; it has become, for many listeners, the original, and the performance its imperfect copy. Some performers have responded by playing more cautiously, aiming at the clean surface that audiences have learned to expect, at the cost of the spontaneity that once distinguished the live event.

It would be wrong to treat this as a simple story of decline. Recording has also allowed listeners to compare interpretations in a way no earlier audience could, and it has preserved musical traditions that might otherwise have vanished with their last practitioners. The point is rather that recording is not neutral. A technology that lets us hear the same performance indefinitely changes what we think a performance is for, and an account of modern musical life that leaves this out has mistaken a transformation for a mere extension.

passage: Most people believe that anything sufficiently striking will catch their eye. If a person in a gorilla suit walked through a game of catch we were watching, we assume we would notice. A well-known series of experiments suggests otherwise. When viewers are asked to count the passes made by one team in a short video, a large share of them fail to see an unexpected figure stroll through the middle of the scene, even when it pauses to face the camera. Asked afterwards, many insist that nothing unusual happened, and some are indignant when the recording is replayed.

The phenomenon, usually called inattentional blindness, is easy to misread as a failure of the eyes. It is not, or at least not in any sense that an optician could detect: the light from the unexpected figure reaches the retina as surely as the light from the ball. What fails is the selection that decides which parts of the scene will be built into conscious experience. Attention is not a spotlight that merely brightens what we are looking at; it is closer to a gate, and what does not pass through the gate is not dimly seen but, for practical purposes, not seen at all.

The finding matters less because of its surprise value than because of the confidence it exposes. We are poor judges of what we would notice, because the things we miss leave no trace in experience from which we could learn that we missed them. Ordinary experience, which might be expected to correct our overconfidence, cannot do so, because an occasion on which we failed to notice something is, from the inside, indistinguishable from an occasion on which there was nothing to notice. A driver who looks at a junction while thinking about something else may have no sense that a cyclist was in view. Afterwards he will report, quite sincerely, that the cyclist came from nowhere. His honesty is not in question; his access to his own lapse is.

This should not be taken to mean that attention is simply defective. A mind that admitted everything in the visual field to awareness would be overwhelmed, unable to follow the ball, read a page or hold a conversation in a crowded room. Selectivity is the price of focus, and on most days, when little that we fail to notice turns out to matter, the price is low. The lesson is narrower and more practical: where the cost of missing something is high, we should not rely on the conviction that we would have seen it, and should instead design tasks, roads and warning signals on the assumption that attention is already spoken for.

passage: For a long time the standard story about technology and pay was a story about skill. New machines, and computers above all, were thought to complement educated workers and to substitute for the rest, so that demand for the educated rose faster than their supply and the gap between their wages and everyone else's widened. Inequality, in this account, was the outcome of a contest in which schooling had to keep pace with machines, and the remedy was plain: produce more graduates. The story had the virtue of simplicity and the defect of predicting a smooth gradient, with the prospects of jobs improving in proportion to the schooling they required.

What many studies of rich economies in the closing decades of the twentieth century found instead was a hollowing out. Employment grew at the top of the wage distribution and, more surprisingly, at the bottom, while the middle shrank. The explanation that has largely displaced the skill story looks not at workers but at tasks. A computer, on this view, is good at carrying out any procedure that can be fully specified in advance, and the jobs made up mostly of such procedures, keeping ledgers, typing correspondence, inspecting items on a production line, happened to sit in the middle of the wage scale. Jobs at the top require judgement and the framing of problems; many jobs at the bottom, guarding a building, preparing food, helping an elderly person to bathe, require adaptability in physical settings that no program could specify. Neither kind of task was routine, and so both survived.

The task view is a real advance. It explains a pattern the skill view could not, and it shifts attention from the credentials of workers to the content of work. But its central category is less solid than it appears. Whether a task counts as routine is usually settled by asking whether it has in fact been automated, and a classification fixed by results cannot then be used to predict them without circularity. Tasks once thought to demand judgement, such as reading medical images or drafting standard contracts, are now discussed as candidates for automation, and if they are automated they will be relabelled routine after the event. The line between routine and non-routine describes the frontier of a particular technology; it is not a fact about the tasks themselves.

A second difficulty is subtler. Both the skill story and the task story treat technology as an external force that arrives and to which labour markets adjust. Yet which tasks are automated is a decision made by firms, and it depends on what machines cost relative to people, on how the tax system treats investment in equipment compared with spending on wages, and on whether managers regard workers as a cost to be reduced or a capacity to be developed. The same software can be deployed to remove a clerk or to let her handle cases that once needed a specialist. Polarisation, from this angle, is not simply what computers do to jobs; it is partly what a given set of incentives led firms to do with computers.

None of this makes the task view wrong, and it would be careless to replace one tidy determinism with another in which every outcome is a choice. Some tasks really are cheaper to mechanise than others, and no tax code will make a typing pool competitive again. The claim is narrower: that the shape of the wage distribution reflects technology filtered through institutions, and that a theory which treats the filter as fixed will mistake a policy question for a law of nature.

passage: It has become a commonplace that the internet would be a more civil place if people had to speak under their own names. The reasoning is simple: a person who cannot be identified bears no cost for cruelty, and a person who bears no cost will be cruel more often. Proposals to require verified identities on public platforms rest on this reasoning, and it has an obvious appeal to anyone who has read the comments beneath a news article.

The reasoning is not wrong so much as incomplete. Anonymity does loosen some restraints; people say things to a faceless audience that they would not say across a table. But the restraint that matters most in face-to-face life is not the fear of being named. It is the expectation of meeting the same people again. A villager who insults a neighbour must live beside her the next day; a commuter who insults a stranger on a train usually need not, and commuters are not famous for their courtesy. What disinhibits is less the absence of a name than the absence of a future in which one's words will have to be lived with.

Seen this way, the relevant distinction online is not between named and anonymous accounts but between identities that are durable and identities that are disposable. A pseudonym used for years in a small forum accumulates a reputation as surely as a name does, and its owner has much to lose by squandering it. Many such forums are known for patient and generous discussion, though few of their members could be identified by an outsider. Conversely, people posting under their real names on large platforms frequently behave badly, perhaps because the audience is so vast and transient that no particular reader's opinion of them seems to count.

None of this shows that identity requirements would do nothing. They might deter some of the worst abuse, and they would make legal remedies easier to pursue. But they carry costs that fall unevenly. The people with most to fear from being named are not usually the trolls; they are the employee describing misconduct at work, the young person asking about a matter their family would punish, the dissenter in a place where dissent is dangerous. A policy that removes their cover in order to inconvenience the cruel has chosen a blunt instrument where a finer one was available: designing spaces in which identities, named or not, persist long enough to matter.

passage: Almost every modern constitution makes room for its own partial suspension. In a war, an epidemic or a sudden collapse of public order, the executive may be permitted to rule by decree, restrict movement or detain people without the usual procedures, on the understanding that these powers serve to preserve the constitutional order rather than to replace it. The logic is respectable. A constitution that made no provision for emergencies would not prevent governments from acting in a crisis; it would simply ensure that they acted outside the law, improvising powers with no defined limits and no defined end.

The danger that emergency provisions are usually designed to guard against is the dramatic one: a leader who declares a crisis in order to abolish the constitution altogether. That danger is real but comparatively rare. The more common pattern is quieter. An emergency is declared for a genuine reason, and then renewed, and renewed again, because the threat has not entirely disappeared and no official wants to be blamed if it returns. Measures adopted as exceptions are gradually written into ordinary statutes, where they no longer need renewal at all. And each emergency lowers the threshold for the next, since officials and citizens alike grow accustomed to powers that once seemed extraordinary.

The standard remedy is the sunset clause, which makes emergency powers lapse after a fixed period unless they are renewed. Sunset clauses are better than nothing, but they tend to turn renewal into a formality, a vote taken under the shadow of the original fear by legislators who see little to gain from being the ones who let the powers lapse. What matters is not whether powers expire but how hard it is to extend them. A more demanding design would require larger majorities for each successive renewal, so that a measure which commanded a bare majority at the outset needed broad agreement to survive a year later, and it would oblige the government to state publicly, each time, why ordinary law is still inadequate to the threat.

Such designs would not prevent a determined government from abusing emergency powers, and no constitutional text can do that alone; courts, a free press and an opposition willing to make itself unpopular all have parts to play. The purpose of the design is more modest: to make normalisation visible and expensive, so that an exception which has outlasted its reasons must be defended openly as a permanent change rather than slipping into permanence unnoticed. A government that genuinely needs lasting powers can still obtain them, but only by persuading a broad majority that the change should be lasting. The test of an emergency regime is less whether it can survive a coup than whether it can end.

passage: For much of the last century, efforts to explain science to the public rested on a simple picture. People who resisted a scientific conclusion, it was assumed, did so because they did not understand it; the gap between expert and lay opinion was a gap in knowledge, and it could be closed by supplying the missing facts. Critics later gave this picture a name, the deficit model, and the name stuck because it captured what was wrong with it: it treated the public as a vessel with a hole in it, defined entirely by what it lacked.

The model fails first on its own terms. If resistance came from ignorance, those who knew most about a contested subject would be the most accepting of the expert view, yet it is easy to find people who have read widely on a topic and still reject the consensus, sometimes with more conviction than before they began. Knowledge, it turns out, can be recruited to defend a position as readily as to change it. A person who already distrusts the source of a claim does not experience new information as enlightenment; she experiences it as further pressure from that source. The facts are heard, but they are heard as moves in a contest whose sides were chosen before the conversation began.

The deeper failure concerns what the model leaves out. Consider a village told by a team of engineers that a new dam upstream poses no danger. The villagers may follow the hydrology perfectly well. What they also know, and what the engineers' presentation omits, is that the last assurance they received from officials turned out to be wrong, that the benefits of the dam will flow to a distant city, and that if anything goes wrong it is they, not the engineers, who will bear the loss. Their scepticism is not a vacancy waiting to be filled. It is a judgement about whom to trust and who pays, and it may be quite rational even when the hydrology is sound.

None of this means that facts are irrelevant or that every misunderstanding is secretly a stance about power. Some people do hold mistaken beliefs simply because nobody has explained a matter clearly, and for them a good explanation is exactly what is needed. The error of the deficit model was to make this the whole story. Communication that begins by asking what an audience already knows, fears and has experienced will sometimes end in explanation. But it will at least explain the right thing, and it will treat the people it addresses as parties to a decision rather than as containers for information.

passage: Boredom is usually described as a kind of emptiness, the feeling of having nothing to feel. On this view it is a residue, what remains when interest drains away, and the natural response is to fill the space with whatever is at hand, much as one might fill an awkward silence with remarks about the weather. The description is understandable, since boredom rarely announces any object of its own, but it gets the state almost exactly backwards. Boredom is not an absence. It is an active and often insistent signal that the activity in front of us is failing to engage the capacities we have available, and it exists to make us do something about that.

The comparison with other unpleasant states is instructive. Hunger is disagreeable, but nobody concludes from this that hunger is a defect; its discomfort is the means by which it gets us to eat. Boredom works in a similar way. A person bored by a repetitive clerical task does not merely register that the task is dull; she feels restless, glances at the clock, begins to imagine alternatives. The unpleasantness is doing work. It pushes attention away from a situation that offers too little and towards a search for one that offers more, whether that means a harder problem, a different companion or simply a walk.

None of this implies that boredom is always benign. A signal is useful only when there is some way to act on it, and many situations offer none. The patient in a waiting room, the passenger on a delayed train and the worker who cannot leave a monotonous post all receive the message without being able to respond, and in such cases boredom curdles into frustration or something close to despair. There are also signs that people will sometimes reach for almost any stimulation rather than endure an unoccupied mind, even stimulation they would otherwise find unpleasant. The signal, in other words, can be loud enough to drive choices that serve no one, and a theory of boredom that celebrated it without reservation would be as misleading as one that dismissed it.

What follows is a reason to be wary of the most popular remedy. If boredom is a message about the fit between a person and an activity, then an endless supply of small distractions does not answer the message; it merely muffles it. Someone who reaches for a screen at every lull may never feel bored for long, but may also never learn what the boredom was pointing at: a job that has stopped stretching them, a routine that has outlived its purpose, a curiosity that has gone unfed. The more useful question, when boredom arrives, is not how to make it stop but what it is about.

passage: Physicists have long remarked that several of the numbers fixing the behaviour of matter seem oddly well suited to the existence of anything as complicated as a living thing. Were certain forces a little stronger or a little weaker, the argument runs, stars would burn out too quickly or never ignite, atoms heavier than hydrogen would be scarce, and chemistry would offer nothing as intricate as a cell. How tightly these numbers are really constrained is debated, and some claims of extreme precision have not survived scrutiny. Enough of the pattern has held up, however, to pose a question: why should the constants of nature fall within the narrow ranges that permit observers to exist at all?

One family of answers appeals to what is usually called anthropic reasoning. Its modest form makes a point that sounds almost too obvious to state: whatever we observe must be compatible with our being there to observe it. We should not be astonished to find ourselves on a planet with liquid water and a tolerable climate, since observers could hardly have arisen anywhere else; to treat our surroundings as a fair sample of the cosmos would be like concluding that a town's residents are unusually fit because everyone one has met there was met at the swimming pool. In this form the principle is not a theory of anything. It is a warning about bias, and as a warning it is both correct and useful.

The difficulty begins when the same reasoning is asked to explain the constants themselves. Consider a lottery. A winner who learns that millions of tickets were sold need suspect nothing: someone had to win, and the winner is simply whoever did. But if only one ticket was ever printed and it won, the winner's existence explains nothing about why that ticket was drawn; it guarantees only that, had it not been, there would be no winner left to wonder. A selection effect does explanatory work only when there are many draws among which selection can operate. Applied to the cosmos, anthropic reasoning dissolves the puzzle of fine tuning only if there are many universes, or many regions of one, in which the constants take different values, and we necessarily find ourselves in one of the hospitable few.

Defenders of the approach reply that such an ensemble is not invented for the purpose. Some cosmological theories, developed to address quite different problems, appear to imply a vast number of regions with differing properties, and if those theories are right, the anthropic explanation comes, so to speak, free of charge. The reply has force, but it shifts the burden rather than lifting it. The explanation is now exactly as good as the theory that supplies the ensemble, and since the other regions are, on most versions, unobservable in principle, the evidence for that theory must come from somewhere else. Anthropic reasoning cannot certify its own premise.

None of this shows that the approach is unscientific, a charge often levelled against it with more heat than precision. Selection effects are a respectable part of reasoning in every empirical science, and ignoring them produces errors as surely as overrating them does. The narrower lesson is that the modest principle and the ambitious one are different claims and should not borrow each other's credibility. The first is nearly beyond dispute and explains almost nothing on its own; the second would explain a great deal, but only on a condition that the principle itself is powerless to establish.

passage: Students and teachers share a reasonable-sounding rule: if learning feels smooth, it is going well. A chapter reread the night before an examination seems familiar, a set of problems practised one type at a time feels increasingly easy, and the growing ease is taken as proof of mastery. The rule is reasonable because in many activities fluency really does track competence. A pianist who plays a passage without stumbling has, in some sense, learned it. Yet in the specific matter of building knowledge that lasts and transfers, the rule is frequently misleading, and sometimes backwards.

The reason is that the conditions which make performance easy during study are often not the conditions which make memory durable. Rereading produces familiarity, the sense of having seen something before, which is easily mistaken for the ability to recall it unaided. Practising one kind of problem in a block lets the learner apply the same procedure again and again without ever deciding which procedure the problem calls for, the very decision a mixed examination demands. By contrast, spacing study sessions apart, testing oneself instead of rereading, and mixing problem types all make study feel slower and more error-prone, and all tend to produce better retention weeks later. The effort of retrieving a half-forgotten fact, or of working out which method applies, appears to be part of what fixes it in memory.

It would be easy to draw the wrong lesson from this, namely that harder is always better. It is not. A difficulty helps only when the learner can, with effort, overcome it; material pitched far beyond a student's grasp produces confusion rather than consolidation, and a test on something never learned teaches little except discouragement. The useful difficulties are those that call on processes the learner will later need, such as retrieval, discrimination and reconstruction, rather than obstacles that merely slow things down. Printing a textbook in a faint, awkward typeface makes reading harder, but there is little reason to expect it to make anything stick.

The deeper problem is one of judgement. Because learners rely on how study feels, they systematically prefer the methods that serve them worst, and they are not foolish to do so: the costs of effortful methods are felt now, while their benefits arrive later and unannounced. Teachers face a similar temptation, since a lesson in which students struggle looks, to an observer and to the students themselves, like a lesson that has gone badly. Changing practice therefore requires more than information about which methods work. It requires a willingness to distrust a feeling that is usually reliable, in exactly the setting where it is not.
